messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

I am running site occupancy models for four herpetofauna species at a rather large scale. Although they began recently, these monitorings are part of a wider, long term conservation project, with the aim of obtaining long term trends. Global occupancy seems like an ideal indicator to track, allowing us to build trends once we'll have enough years of monitoring.

Although I had planned for dynamic occupancy models, the first result to hand out has to be a simple static model (project funder asks for an annual evolution of the indicator). Now, I've been pondering about the differences between static and dynamic. Especially, I wonder if switching to dynamic model as soon as possible (e.g. after two years of monitoring) is such a good idea: does it perform as well with very few years?

If I have multiple years of monitoring available, is it theoretically acceptable to simply run static models for each year (with the same covariates) and then make out a trend of the yearly sample occupancies?

I am sorry if these questions are basic, but if you have any insight I would be very grateful!

Vincent

messages.body_plain:
Dear Vincent,

couple of comments here:
At a certain level, the two models (dynamic, year-stratified/multiple static) give you exactly the same thing: annual occupancy
But they are different in their complexity: the dynamic model is more complex, while the year-stratified model is less so. According to Occam’s razor, the latter is to be preferred, everything else equal
However, the dynamic model accounts for what is likely to be present very often in such data: temporal autocorrelation. Plus, to obtain these yearly estimates of occupancy, the dynocc model uses more information: via the Markovian structure the estimates in each year are informed not only by the data from that specific year, but also by all years before and after. So, the year “indexes” (represented by the annual occupancy) are likely to be better from the dynocc model
The question about how good the estimates of the dynamic rates (extinction/persistence, colonization) are, is a different one. Some people say that with just 2-3 years of data you shouldn’t believe too much the estimates of the dynamic rates. I don’t know.
But in summary I would say that I would prefer the estimates from the dynamic model
And yes, you can fit a linear regression model into the annual estimates of occupancy, see Weir et al. http://www.herpconbio.org/Volume_4/Issue_3/Weir_etal_2009.pdf

Best regards  --- Marc

messages.body_plain:
Hi Vincent,

We have been running long-term annual occupancy-based monitoring programs for several listed species for 10-20 years now.  We use simple single year models for the occupancy trend metric every year.  We used to also run  single and multi-year models every year with covariates as they are both very informative.  However, for cost efficiency, we recently changed to running multi-season models every 3-5 years to get updated information on predictors of colonization and extinction (frequency depends upon variation in climate/ disturbance/management/ etc.) -- and single-year models with covariates each year in between. Our target species are very dynamic, so you may find another strategy works better for your system.

The only issue with what Marc proposed (in our case) - is that the clients don't like when annual trend metric estimates from past years change due to new analyses each year, which is why we produce them independently each year for our annual reports.  But if it's for a manuscript or synthesis report, it sounds like estimates from the dynamic model are better.

Best,
Cheryl

Given the statement "The only issue with what Marc proposed (in our case) - is that the clients don't like when annual trend metric estimates from past years change due to new analyses each year, which is why we produce them independently each year for our annual reports." I'm going to argue that you're unnecessarily missing out on potential explanatory information by doing so and that the annual estimates don't have to change.

If treating years separately is OK, then certainly including separate extinction and colonization probabilities for each transition and separate detection probabilities for each year should be OK and give you exactly the same annual estimates but with a more complete assessment of the annual changes (i.e., estimates of the transition probabilities).  In other words, for extinction, colonization, and detection there would be an interaction with year.  You're already doing that with the detection probabilities for the separate annual estimates.  (Where there are differences - and those would be very small -  I'd argue that's only because of the iterative procedures ending too soon and being slightly different between occu and colext.)  (I wouldn't like to be wrong in this but if I am, please feel free to point that out.  However, it is certainly true for 2 seasons.)

I suppose I should produce some datasets and R code where that is the case to back up my claim.  (I'll do so in the next few days.)

Jim

messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone!

I have a problem with a dynamic occupancy model in JAGS.

I am analyzing camera-trap data from large mammals and checking for environmental and anthropogenic effects.
I have a properly working model, however, when I applied the goodness-of-fit test, some species had very bad results.
As an attempt to maybe make it better, I decided maybe I can add a camera-trap effort variable to the detection probability and see if the model is improving.

So I have a camera-trap activity table showing how many days a camera worked in a month.
In the model my primary occasions are seasons (Winter/Summer) and my secondary occasions are months (Summer: May-June-July-Aug-Sept-Oct and Winter: Dec-Jan-Feb-March - I dropped aprils and novembers to give the animals transition time).

So I wanted to create a "ndays" variable from my camera-trap activity table, and according to my primary/secondary occasion structure, I created this variable as the total number of days that a camera was active per season.

One other thing to note is, since I have a lot of NAs in my camera-trap data, previous versions of the models would either stuck or take a really long time. Therefore, instead of giving a huge matrix (site by season) full of NAs to the model, I am giving an observation vector. Thus, each of the parameters I am putting in the observation model is also according to this vector, so that model knows in which season and site that observation occurred. So I created this "ndays" variable for effort according to this again.

Then I wrote the observation model as: (you can also see the previous version (without ndays))

# Observation model

for (i in 1:nobs){
  logit(p[i]) <- alphap[habitat.p[i]] + betap[habitat.p[i]]*season.p[site[i]]  + randomp[area.p[i]]

   # y[i] ~ dbern(z[site[i],pocc[i]]*p[i])  # previous model of the observed occupancy

    pstar[i] <- 1-(1-p[i])^ndays[i]
    y[i] ~ dbern(z[site[i],pocc[i]]*pstar[i])  # y: observed occupancy
}

Here p should be the daily detection probability, and pstar should be seasonal (according to my primary occasion).
However, this model does not work. It gives the "Node inconsistent with parents" error, and I cannot put my finger on what is the problem?
When I remove the "ndays" variable it works again or when I put the "ndays" variable simply as a covariate in the logit(p) model as and do as:

# Observation model

messages.body_plain:
Dear Tobias,

your model is overparameterized, i.e., you try to estimate too many parameters. This is a typical linear modeling problem: how to parameterize a model with two categorical explanatory variables (in the old times called a 2-way ANOVA). In practice, you have to set to zero some parameters, and the default when fitting such a model in R or probably about any other stats program except for SPSS is to set to zero the parameter(s) associated with the first level of a factor; this requires you have a separate intercept, too. In that case, the intercept becomes the parameter for level 1 of every factor and the other levels are expressed as a difference from that reference. Exactly as what one would do when fitting models in R with lm() or glm().

Best regards  -- Marc

messages.body_plain:
Hi Jim,

Thanks so much for the clarification and example.

For our programs, we run the simple occupancy model each year to produce the annual monitoring trend metric (area occupied).  In trying to keep my initial comment simple, I failed to specify that we also include a small suite of covariates that are known to affect detection probabilities- and also include simple covariates for subpopulations in order to track trends in specific areas- which gets to your point on shared covariates in multi-year models and potential small changes in annual results using dynamic models.  However, in addition to these annual trend metrics, we also regularly run both single and multi-year models and explore explanatory covariates of occ/col/ext parameters.  We simply now do this on a schedule as previously stated for cost efficiency.  We may also run multi-year models more frequently if needed when there are substantial changes in occupancy, large disturbance events, habitat management actions, etc.  Often, the changes in occupancy due to these events were predictable based on previous model results.

After 10-20 years of our long-term monitoring programs, it has been interesting to see annual differences in explanatory covariates for occupancy among years for our target species using single-year models, which give us some extra information that may not be apparent over very long time periods using multi-year models (which we still run on a fairly frequent basis!).

Best,
Cheryl

Below is an example that results in (essentially) the same estimates of annual occupancy from running years separately in occu or in a single analysis in  colext when there are no shared parameters among years.  The very small differences (i.e. agreement to 5 decimal places) are due to different settings in the under-the-hood optimization routines as theoretically they are identical.  This is in response to a comment made that there is a difference in results.  Note that there will likely be differences in results if there are shared parameters among years.

fm <- colext(~1, ~0 + year, ~0 + year, ~0 + year, umf)

# Convert logits to probabilities
  psi1.colext <- 1 - 1/(1+exp(fm@opt$par[1]))
  colonization <- 1 - 1/(1+exp(fm@opt$par[2:4]))
  extinction <- 1 - 1/(1+exp(fm@opt$par[5:7]))

  psi3.colext <- psi2*(1-extinction[2]) + (1-psi2)*colonization[2]
  psi4.colext <- psi3*(1-extinction[3]) + (1-psi3)*colonization[3]

# Now run occu

  ufo1 <- unmarkedFrameOccu(y=y[,  1: 3])
  ufo2 <- unmarkedFrameOccu(y=y[,  4: 6])
  ufo3 <- unmarkedFrameOccu(y=y[,  7: 9])
  ufo4 <- unmarkedFrameOccu(y=y[, 10:12])

  psi1.occu <- 1 - 1/(1+exp(occu(~1 ~1, ufo1)@opt$par[1]))
  psi2.occu <- 1 - 1/(1+exp(occu(~1 ~1, ufo2)@opt$par[1]))
  psi3.occu <- 1 - 1/(1+exp(occu(~1 ~1, ufo3)@opt$par[1]))
  psi4.occu <- 1 - 1/(1+exp(occu(~1 ~1, ufo4)@opt$par[1]))

# Compare results

I'm going to argue that you're unnecessarily missing out on potential explanatory information by doing so and that the annual estimates don't have to change.

Dear all,

Registration is now open, please visit http://www.phidot.org/euring/ for information. Fees are 250 euros for in person attendance, including access to the conference, lunches, icebreaker, excursions, diner gala, and workshops (excluding accommodation), and 50 euros for remote attendance. Deadline for registration is February 10, 2023.

Alison Johnston https://www.st-andrews.ac.uk/mathematics-statistics/people/ap48/

Vital rate estimation
Movement & dispersal
Software & custom estimation approaches
Management & conservation
Causal inference and decision science
Species distributions
Phenology

Species interactions & density dependence

Hello Dilsad,
here are some thoughts.
I see that the ndays variable is a very big number(mean=114.52) , when you take a probability p and do 1-(1-p)^114 it will become very quick 1. This may be very restrictive for the model and it may find it very hard to reach convergence.
There are some cases where ndays is zero and p^0=1. So I understand that if ndays is zero it may be because is either broken or not detected, but in the end, the probability will be one. So it is like a mixed message for the mode.

This may not be the root of the error that you present, but may facilitate the convergence of the model in the future.

>

> I am attaching the full model code and the sample data to run it.
>
> I'd be appreciated if anyone has any ideas and sorry for the long post! 🐒

> Thank you in advance!

messages.body_plain:
Hi Diego,

Thanks for your input.

You were right about your 1st point.
I solved the issue (thanks to some discussions with Thomas Riecke in the group) by changing the prior of mean detection (alphap) from dlogis(0,1) to dlogis(-2,1).
Another option I found is diluting the ndays variable by doing something like ndays/10, however this would be a little hard for interpretation, because it would mean "detection probability of every 10 days" which is a little weird thing to do. Therefore I'm going with changing alphap prior option now.

For your 2nd point, I think ndays=0 shouldn't be a problem, because it is coded as
pstar = 1 - (1-p)^ndays
so when ndays=0, pstar (monthly detection) is also 0. So that would make sense.

Thank you so much again!
Best,
Dilsad

Hi everyone, thanks a lot for this much appreciated input.

I'm trying to sum up your different infos and advices. Given that I will have shared parameters on top of years (for occ and det at least), it appears that either I should make clear to the client that the metric might change with each new analyse and go with a dynamic model that takes in account temporal correlation, or if the client want an indicator that doesn't change with each new analyse, go with Cheryl's method of year-stratified static models with a dynamic model every once in a while to explore and refine dynamic parameters.

Dear Cheryl, it seems to me that what you are doing is quite close to what I should do, thanks for sharing your experience! This may be a bit off-topic, but when you say that you "also include simple covariates for subpopulations in order to track trends in specific areas", I guess you mean that your statistical sample has been properly stratified to allow it to be divided into smaller portions (subpopulations), in which to keep track of the indicator at a smaller spatial scale (by the mean of a "region covariate" associated with each site maybe). Do you run these covariates for subpopulations in multi-year models as well, and has it ever given you a different trend than the year-stratified method?

Thanks so much,
Vincent

> Thanks so much for the clarification and example.
>
> For our programs, we run the simple occupancy model each year to produce the annual monitoring trend metric (area occupied).  In trying to keep my initial comment simple, I failed to specify that we also include a small suite of covariates that are known to affect detection probabilities- and also include simple covariates for subpopulations in order to track trends in specific areas- which gets to your point on shared covariates in multi-year models and potential small changes in annual results using dynamic models.  However, in addition to these annual trend metrics, we also regularly run both single and multi-year models and explore explanatory covariates of occ/col/ext parameters.  We simply now do this on a schedule as previously stated for cost efficiency.  We may also run multi-year models more frequently if needed when there are substantial changes in occupancy, large disturbance events, habitat management actions, etc.  Often, the changes in occupancy due to these events were predictable based on previous model results.
>
> After 10-20 years of our long-term monitoring programs, it has been interesting to see annual differences in explanatory covariates for occupancy among years for our target species using single-year models, which give us some extra information that may not be apparent over very long time periods using multi-year models (which we still run on a fairly frequent basis!).

> > Given the statement "The only issue with what Marc proposed (in our case) - is that the clients don't like when annual trend metric estimates from past years change due to new analyses each year, which is why we produce them independently each year for our annual reports." I'm going to argue that you're unnecessarily missing out on potential explanatory information by doing so and that the annual estimates don't have to change.
> >
> > If treating years separately is OK, then certainly including separate extinction and colonization probabilities for each transition and separate detection probabilities for each year should be OK and give you exactly the same annual estimates but with a more complete assessment of the annual changes (i.e., estimates of the transition probabilities). messages.body_plain:
Hi Matt,

Thank you for your reply.
The previous version of the model was working fine only with initial values on z (true occupancy), but I didn't try the new version with initial values on p.
But I think the issue was, when I add the ndays in the code as I shared above, and when the mean detection prior was dlogis(0,1) JAGS was estimating monthly detection to be close to 1 all the time and this was creating a discrepancy between the estimates and the data. That's why I went on with changing the prior to dlogis(-2,1).
This solution makes more sense to me than try to find the suitable initial values, because I know that my detection in the area is low anyway, so lowering the mean detection probability value by changing the prior made more sense.

Best,
Dilsad

On Mon, Nov 14, 2022 at 11:59 AM Matthijs Hollanders <matthijs....@gmail.com> wrote:
> Hi Dilsad,
>
> Pretty sure it’s an initial values problem. Have you tried initialising the detection parameters (and perhaps others) to suitable values?
>
> Matt
>
> On Mon, 14 Nov 2022 at 21:08, Dilsad Dagtekin <dils...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Hi Diego,
> >
> > Thanks for your input.
> >
> > You were right about your 1st point.
> > I solved the issue (thanks to some discussions with Thomas Riecke in the group) by changing the prior of mean detection (alphap) from dlogis(0,1) to dlogis(-2,1).
> > Another option I found is diluting the ndays variable by doing something like ndays/10, however this would be a little hard for interpretation, because it would mean "detection probability of every 10 days" which is a little weird thing to do. Therefore I'm going with changing alphap prior option now.
> >
> > For your 2nd point, I think ndays=0 shouldn't be a problem, because it is coded as
> > pstar = 1 - (1-p)^ndays
> > so when ndays=0, pstar (monthly detection) is also 0. So that would make sense.
> >
> > Thank you so much again!
> > Best,
> > Dilsad
> >
> > On Mon, Nov 14, 2022 at 10:07 AM Diego Rondon <diegoro...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > Hello Dilsad,
> > > here are some thoughts.
> > > I see that the ndays variable is a very big number(mean=114.52) , when you take a probability p and do 1-(1-p)^114 it will become very quick 1. This may be very restrictive for the model and it may find it very hard to reach convergence.
> > > There are some cases where ndays is zero and p^0=1. So I understand that if ndays is zero it may be because is either broken or not detected, but in the end, the probability will be one. So it is like a mixed message for the mode.
> > >
> > > This may not be the root of the error that you present, but may facilitate the convergence of the model in the future.
> > >

> > > > Hi everyone!
> > > >

> > > >

Hi Vincent,

Actually, I haven't rerun estimates of annual occupancy for each of the subpopulations using multi-year models for a while since I didn't see the need (although I can try that next time around—in that case the detection probability covariates will be shared among years so will expect minor variations of estimates).  However, with 10-20 years of data with up and down trends, I would need to use a subpop*year interaction term for annual occupancy estimates which could potentially result in over-parameterization issues. For multi-year models, we typically focus on assessing landscape, habitat, co-occurring species, and climate covariates to better understand temporal species dynamics to these and to inform habitat management.  However, for one project with high sample sizes, along with region-wide multi-year models, I also run dynamic models for specific subpopulations to see if predictors of colonization and extinction differ among them...and yes, our sampling for these are all probabilistic and optimized/stratified for trends within and across populations.  I see you have bufo in your email address and one of our projects is for a listed toad species for which we also include hydrological variables.  Please feel free to contact me directly if you would like to discuss further.

Best,
Cheryl

Hi everyone, thanks a lot for this much appreciated input.

I'm trying to sum up your different infos and advices. Given that I will have shared parameters on top of years (for occ and det at least), it appears that either I should make clear to the client that the metric might change with each new analyse and go with a dynamic model that takes in account temporal correlation, or if the client want an indicator that doesn't change with each new analyse, go with Cheryl's method of year-stratified static models with a dynamic model every once in a while to explore and refine dynamic parameters.

Dear Cheryl, it seems to me that what you are doing is quite close to what I should do, thanks for sharing your experience! This may be a bit off-topic, but when you say that you "also include simple covariates for subpopulations in order to track trends in specific areas", I guess you mean that your statistical sample has been properly stratified to allow it to be divided into smaller portions (subpopulations), in which to keep track of the indicator at a smaller spatial scale (by the mean of a "region covariate" associated with each site maybe). Do you run these covariates for subpopulations in multi-year models as well, and has it ever given you a different trend than the year-stratified method?

Thanks so much,
Vincent

Dear Alaa,

and what exactly is your question ?

Basically, in your model adding a covariate on detection prob p will produce the form of a logistic regression exactly as for the models on psi1, gamma and phi on your model. That is,  you can add a covariate with as many values as you have years t, in your formulation of the model. And then you write something like this in the likelihood:

  for(t in 1:nYears) {
   p[t] <- ilogit(lp[t])

   lp[t] <- alpha.lp + beta.lp * cov[t]
  }

As for priors, I like to give a U(0,1) on the intercept of a logistic regression in the inverse-link scale. That is:

alpha.lp <- logit(mean.p)

mean.p ~ dunif(0, 1)

Then, for the coefficient beta, this is a real number that may a priori be either positive or negative. Hence, I’d give a prior like one of these:

beta.lp ~ dunif(-5, 5)         or

beta.lp ~ dnorm(0, 0.01)

I note that in your code below, I don’t think that the priors for the covariates on the other parameters make sense, since you constrain them to live on 0 to 1. I’d choose some prior for them as what I suggest here for the covariate in a model for p.

Best regards  -- Marc

I'm sure it is a very naive question, but I'm also very naive about the Jags and how to write scripts.

 I'm modelling species occupancy using the dynamic occupancy model. I wonder how to include a variable on detection probability and its prior.

I use the below code and an example of jags data (jdata) is attached as a reproducible example.

Your help is really appreciated

cat("
model{
  for(i in 1:nSites) {
    # biological process
    lpsi1[i] <- lpsiInt + bpsi*SST[i]
    psi1[i] <- ilogit(lpsi1[i])
    z[i, 1] ~ dbern(psi1[i])
    for(t in 2:nYears) {
      lphi[i, t-1] <- lphiInt[t-1] + bphi*SST[i]
      phi[i, t-1] <- ilogit(lphi[i, t-1])
      lgam[i, t-1] <- lgamInt[t-1] +  bgam*SST[i]

    }
    # detection process
    for(t in 1:nYears) {
     y[i, t] ~ dbin(p[t] * z[i, t], n[i, t])

    }
  }

  # Priors
  psiInt ~ dbeta(1, 1)
  lpsiInt <- logit(psiInt)

  for(t in 1:(nYears-1)) {
    phiInt[t] ~ dbeta(1, 1)
    lphiInt[t] <- logit(phiInt[t])
    gamInt[t] ~ dbeta(1, 1)
    lgamInt[t] <- logit(gamInt[t])
  }

  for(t in 1:nYears) {
    p[t] ~ dbeta(1, 1)
  }

  bpsi ~ dunif(0,1)
  bphi ~ dunif(0,1)
  bgam ~ dunif(0,1)

  # Derived variable
  for(t in 1:nYears) {
    N[t] <- sum(z[,t]) # no. sites occupied for each year
  }
}", fill=TRUE, file="dynoccSST.text")

messages.subject_clean: Dealing with uneven number of visits when using palaeontological data
messages.body_plain:
Hi everyone,

Apologies for anyone in the unmarked group for the crosspost - just posting in here to cover my bases. I’m also going to preface this by saying I’m very new to occupancy modelling in general, so apologies if there is a simple answer to this!

To give some background, I’m a palaeontologist who’s become interested in occupancy modelling as a way to better understand the factors influencing preservation in the fossil record. In my current project, I’m attempting to apply some single season occupancy models to a dataset of dinosaur occurrences from the end Cretaceous using unmarked to answer questions about how the fossil record influences perceived patterns prior to the end Cretaceous mass extinction at 66 million years ago. Asides from a few papers, occupancy modelling hasn’t really caught on in palaeo yet, so I’m unsure about how to setup my data considering the peculiarities of fossil data.

In terms of my setup, I’ve downloaded North American fossil occurrences from the paleobiology database (http://paleobiodb.org for those interested), which contains presence only records of fossil occurrences reported in ‘collections’ (basically a collecting event from a distinct rock horizon/geologic time at a specific geographic locality). Collections can have one or many fossils occurrences within them. I have then used R to grid up collections from the same time intervals into both 0.1 or 0.5 degree grids, with the aim of testing these datasets in different occupancy models. I am using these grid cells as my ‘sites’, and then each collection is a ‘visit’, with the presence of my target taxon within each collection as a detection, and the absence of it as a non-detection. This is similar to how I’ve seen some occupancy approaches deal with historical data not specifically collected for occupancy modelling, and also similar to some other palaeo papers that have used occupancy modelling.

However, my issue comes with the fact that I have a strongly uneven number of visits between sites, which is introducing an enormous amount of NAs in the site by species matrix. To give an example, the majority of my sites (grid cells) have between 1-3 collections in them, but maybe 5% of them have between 80-130 collections. This obviously is extremely skewed, and I’ve read elsewhere that having such uneven numbers of visits can cause problems for the model through the introduction of NAs. As such, I’ve been trying to decide on a way to deal with it, and I’ve come up with a number of options:

Leave it, and accept that this might cause issues (definitely not my preferred method!).
Truncation of sites. There’s a paper (Lawing, A.M., Blois, J.L., Maguire, K.C., Goring, S.J., Wang, Y. and McGuire, J.L., 2021. Occupancy models reveal regional differences in detectability and improve relative abundance estimations in fossil pollen assemblages. Quaternary Science Reviews, 253, p.106747) that’s applied occupancy modelling to fossil pollen records, which also had issues with uneven ‘visits’ between ‘sites’ (although their setup differed from mine due to their data types). To deal with this, they introduced a cut off of 10 ‘visits’, and removed any further visits from their matrix. They found that this improved model results, but I was somewhat unsure of the validity of removing any visits after the first 10 or so.
Remove those sites. Another possibility would just be removing any sites which have a vastly larger number of visits. However, fossil data is already fairly sparce, and I would then be losing a large amount of potentially valuable information.
Subsample/make ‘average’ occupancy. My final thought was to effectively create an ‘average’ detection history. I wrote a quick script in R that randomly samples the detection history of a site with more visits than a specified limit (e.g. 10 visits per site) 1000 times to generate an ‘average’ detection history. However, this obviously means I can’t attach observation level detection covariates within this model. I also thought about randomly sampling a specific number of visits and just running the model, but then each model would have to be run many times to create an ‘average’, and interpreting the results from that would be very problematic.

As you can see, I am unsure of the best procedure to use, or whether any of these options make sense. I am also unsure of whether this is a also indicative of a larger issue of spatial auto-correction, and whether that should be incorporated in my model somehow.

Does anyone have any suggestions or thoughts on what the best course of action for me may be?

Thanks so much for reading (sorry this ended up so long!), and if you have any questions just let me know and I’ll do my best to clarify for you!

Best wishes,

Chris

Asides from a few papers, occupancy modelling hasn’t really caught on in palaeo yet, so I’m unsure about how to setup my data considering the peculiarities of fossil data.

In terms of my setup, I’ve downloaded North American fossil occurrences from the paleobiology database (http://paleobiodb.org for those interested), which contains presence only records of fossil occurrences reported in ‘collections’ (basically a collecting event from a distinct rock horizon/geologic time at a specific geographic locality). Collections can have one or many fossils occurrences within them. I have then used R to grid up collections from the same time intervals into both 0.1 or 0.5 degree grids, with the aim of testing these datasets in different occupancy models. I am using these grid cells as my ‘sites’, and then each collection is a ‘visit’, with the presence of my target taxon within each collection as a detection, and the absence of it as a non-detection. This is similar to how I’ve seen some occupancy approaches deal with historical data not specifically collected for occupancy modelling, and also similar to some other palaeo papers that have used occupancy modelling.

However, my issue comes with the fact that I have a strongly uneven number of visits between sites, which is introducing an enormous amount of NAs in the site by species matrix. To give an example, the majority of my sites (grid cells) have between 1-3 collections in them, but maybe 5% of them have between 80-130 collections. This obviously is extremely skewed, and I’ve read elsewhere that having such uneven numbers of visits can cause problems for the model through the introduction of NAs. As such, I’ve been trying to decide on a way to deal with it, and I’ve come up with a number of options:
Leave it, and accept that this might cause issues (definitely not my preferred method!).
Truncation of sites. There’s a paper (Lawing, A.M., Blois, J.L., Maguire, K.C., Goring, S.J., Wang, Y. and McGuire, J.L., 2021. Occupancy models reveal regional differences in detectability and improve relative abundance estimations in fossil pollen assemblages. Quaternary Science Reviews, 253, p.106747) that’s applied occupancy modelling to fossil pollen records, which also had issues with uneven ‘visits’ between ‘sites’ (although their setup differed from mine due to their data types). To deal with this, they introduced a cut off of 10 ‘visits’, and removed any further visits from their matrix. They found that this improved model results, but I was somewhat unsure of the validity of removing any visits after the first 10 or so.
Remove those sites. Another possibility would just be removing any sites which have a vastly larger number of visits. However, fossil data is already fairly sparce, and I would then be losing a large amount of potentially valuable information.
Subsample/make ‘average’ occupancy. My final thought was to effectively create an ‘average’ detection history. I wrote a quick script in R that randomly samples the detection history of a site with more visits than a specified limit (e.g. 10 visits per site) 1000 times to generate an ‘average’ detection history. However, this obviously means I can’t attach observation level detection covariates within this model. I also thought about randomly sampling a specific number of visits and just running the model, but then each model would have to be run many times to create an ‘average’, and interpreting the results from that would be very problematic.

As you can see, I am unsure of the best procedure to use, or whether any of these options make sense. I am also unsure of whether this is a also indicative of a larger issue of spatial auto-correction, and whether that should be incorporated in my model somehow.

Does anyone have any suggestions or thoughts on what the best course of action for me may be?

Thanks so much for reading (sorry this ended up so long!), and if you have any questions just let me know and I’ll do my best to clarify for you!

Best wishes,

Chris
